newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish banks' bond portfolios bear risk - banker.
newsitem.headline: Turkish banks' bond portfolios bear risk - banker.

text.p: The Treasury bill and bond portfolios of Turkish banks pose greater risk for the banking system and economy than their foreign currency positions, Orhan Emirdag, general manager of Pamukbank, a leading private bank, said.
"The short (currency) positions in the system are manageable but some banks in the system carry fairly higher risks with their treasury-bill and bond portfolios," he told Reuters.
Emirdag said short currency positions stood at between $2.5 to $3.0 billion, far below the $5.0 to $5.5 billion estimated during the 1994 financial and economic crises.

T-bill and bond portfolios of banks almost tripled to 686.7 trillion lira on December 6 from 258.4 trillion at the end of 1995. Outstanding domestic debt was 2,958 trillion lira at end-November, compared to 1,361 at end-1995.

Banks made good profits from t-bill and bond portfolios and trade, as reflected in nine-month reports, due to high real interest rates of up to 40 percent. The year-on-year inflation rate is running at around 80 percent.
He said most of the small members of the system made big profits. But the large banks which depend more on deposits for liquidity are against high real interest rates.
He said most of the small banks made good profits from bonds by carrying higher risk than they should.
"But if the interest rates on t-bills and bonds soar suddenly, the cost of emptying the bond portfolios will be very high," Emirdag said.
Emirdag was optimistic about the Turkish economy in 1997, if the government did not make serious mistakes.
He said an austerity program was still needed to deal with huge deficits. Re-establishing relations with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) should be considered within such a program.
Turkey and the IMF are expected to resume talks in late January or early February.
"A green light from the IMF will help Turkey to correct the recent downgradings by the international rating agencies," Emirdag said.
Emirdag said Pamukbank's 1997 targets were ambitious, including another real increase in total assets which rose to $3.2 billion this year from $2.5 billion in 1995.
The bank targets to increase by 150 percent its call-deposits in 1997, which is the main profit-producing element for banks amid Turkey's inflationary environment.

Pamukbank, active both in commercial and private banking, is Turkey's fourth biggest private bank in terms of assets. Emirdag said the bank was among the top three in overall ranking of private banking activies.
